scenario: You were recently promoted to manage your former peers. One team member, who also applied for the role, has been making passive-aggressive comments in team meetings and undermining your directives. How do you handle this?

options.text: Schedule a private 1-on-1 to openly acknowledge the awkwardness, validate their feelings, and discuss how you can work together productively.
Ignore the comments for now, hoping they will naturally adjust to the new dynamic over time.
Remind them of your new authority during the next team meeting to establish your leadership position.
Ask your own manager to speak with them about maintaining professionalism in the workplace.

scenario: Your department is rolling out a new software system that requires more data entry. Your team is frustrated and complains that it is a waste of time. How do you gain their buy-in?

options.text: Explain the long-term benefits of the tool for the team and company, and ask for their feedback on making the transition smoother.
Tell them that upper management is forcing this change and they simply have to comply.
Offer to do the data entry for them temporarily until they feel more comfortable with the new system.
Acknowledge their frustration and promise to advocate for a streamlined process in the next management meeting.

scenario: Company-wide budget cuts have led to a freeze on annual bonuses. Team morale has plummeted, and productivity is starting to drop. What is your best course of action?

options.text: Host a transparent team discussion acknowledging the disappointment, then pivot to setting achievable short-term goals to rebuild momentum.
Express your own anger about the cuts to show the team you are on their side.
Try to distract the team by organizing a low-cost social event like a potluck lunch.
Send a memo reminding the team that their job security is the real priority right now.

scenario: A highly experienced veteran on your team has become disengaged. They do their work accurately but refuse to mentor newer staff or participate in brainstorming sessions. How do you re-engage them?

options.text: Meet with them privately to learn what motivates them now, and offer them a specialized role leading a specific, high-level project.
Point out their lack of engagement in their next performance review and mandate they mentor junior staff.
Leave them alone; as long as their core work is done, their lack of participation isn't a major issue.
Ask them casually if there is anything you can do to make their day-to-day work more interesting.

scenario: You need a cross-functional peer manager to allocate their team's resources to your project, but they are hesitant due to their own tight deadlines. How do you influence them?

options.text: Present a clear business case highlighting how your project aligns with their team's goals and offer to trade resources or adjust timelines to ease their burden.
Escalate the issue to the department director immediately to force their compliance.
Keep emailing them reminders about the importance of your project until they yield.
Ask to meet for coffee to build rapport and gently pitch the project again, asking what it would take for them to agree.

scenario: One of your direct reports constantly dominates team meetings, preventing quieter team members from sharing their ideas. How do you handle this to build a more inclusive team environment?

options.text: Speak to the dominating employee privately, praising their enthusiasm but asking for their help in drawing out ideas from quieter team members.
Implement a strict 'round-robin' rule where everyone must speak in turn, strictly enforcing time limits.
Interrupt the dominating employee during the meeting and tell them to give others a chance to speak.
Stop holding team brainstorming sessions and just ask for ideas via email instead.

scenario: You want to delegate a high-visibility presentation to a junior team member to help them grow, but they are nervous and lack confidence. How do you influence them to take the opportunity?

options.text: Explain why you chose them, outline the support you will provide, and offer to co-present the first few slides to build their confidence.
Tell them they have to do it because it's required for their career progression.
Back down and do the presentation yourself to avoid causing them unnecessary stress.
Give them the assignment but schedule multiple practice runs with you so they are fully prepared.

scenario: Two of your team members are in a heated conflict over who gets credit for a recently completed, successful project. How do you resolve this while maintaining your leadership?

options.text: Bring both into a mediated discussion to clarify their specific contributions and establish clearer ownership boundaries for future projects.
Tell them to work it out between themselves, as you expect them to act like professionals.
Divide the credit exactly 50/50 in your report, regardless of the actual work done, to keep the peace.
Meet with them individually to hear their sides, then make a final decision on how to attribute the success.

scenario: Your team has been working in silos, rarely communicating with each other, which has led to duplicated efforts. How do you influence them to collaborate?

options.text: Introduce brief daily stand-ups to share updates and assign a joint project that requires them to rely on each other's expertise.
Send a strong email demanding that everyone cc the entire team on all communications going forward.
Wait for the next duplicated effort to happen, then use it as a harsh example in a team meeting.
Start hosting weekly team lunches to encourage organic conversation and relationship building.

scenario: A high-performing employee is demanding a promotion that you know they are not ready for due to a lack of soft skills. How do you navigate this?

options.text: Acknowledge their hard work, clearly explain the specific soft skills needed for the next level, and create a targeted development plan with them.
Tell them 'no' firmly, explaining that their interpersonal skills are currently too weak.
Give them a small title change without a pay raise to keep them happy in the short term.
Tell them you will put in a good word with HR, but warn them the process takes a long time.

scenario: Your team made a significant error on a client deliverable. Your boss is furious and demands to know who is responsible. How do you respond?

options.text: Take full responsibility as the manager, explain the root cause of the error, and outline the immediate steps you are taking to fix it and prevent recurrence.
Give your boss the name of the employee who made the mistake so they can be held appropriately accountable.
Apologize profusely and assure your boss that you will severely reprimand the entire team.
State that the process was flawed, deflecting direct blame, and propose a new workflow to your boss.

scenario: You need to present a controversial new strategy to your team. You know a few vocal members will immediately push back. How do you prepare?

options.text: Meet with the vocal members individually before the group meeting to preview the strategy, hear their concerns, and incorporate their feedback where possible.
Present the strategy enthusiastically and shut down any negative comments immediately to maintain control of the room.
Deliver the presentation via email instead of a meeting so they don't have a platform to complain.
Present the strategy to the team but leave plenty of time at the end for an open Q&A session.

scenario: You notice a culture of gossip developing within your team, which is damaging trust. How do you leverage your leadership to stop it?

options.text: Address the behavior broadly in a team meeting regarding professional standards, and address specific known instigators in private 1-on-1s.
Send out a copy of the company's code of conduct and highlight the section on harassment.
Ignore it; getting involved in workplace drama will only make you look petty.
Pull aside the subjects of the gossip and offer them emotional support.

scenario: Upper management abruptly changes the scope of a project your team has been working on for weeks, rendering much of their work useless. How do you deliver this news?

options.text: Call a meeting to explain the 'why' behind the business decision, validate their frustration, and immediately pivot to defining clear next steps for the new scope.
Blame upper management for the poor planning so the team doesn't direct their anger at you.
Focus only on the new tasks and avoid mentioning the wasted work to keep things positive.
Apologize deeply for the wasted time and promise to buy the team lunch as compensation.

scenario: A talented employee is highly introverted and rarely speaks up. You believe their insights are crucial. How do you empower them to share?

options.text: Ask them privately how they prefer to communicate, and offer alternatives like sharing ideas via email before meetings or having you present their thoughts with credit.
Call on them directly without warning during the next meeting so they are forced to participate.
Wait for their performance review to mention that they need to be more vocal to succeed.
Give them the agenda a day early so they have time to prepare their thoughts before the meeting.

scenario: You are managing a remote worker who has started missing minor deadlines and turning their camera off during all meetings. How do you address this?

options.text: Schedule a check-in to express care for their well-being, share your observations gently, and ask if there are blockers you can help clear.
Send a formal warning email noting the missed deadlines and mandating camera usage.
Start micromanaging their daily tasks by requiring end-of-day progress reports.
Bring up the missed deadlines in a 1-on-1, but let the camera issue slide for now.

scenario: A direct report bypasses you and takes a minor complaint directly to your manager. How do you handle this breach of chain-of-command?

options.text: Discuss the situation calmly with the employee, explain the importance of addressing issues together first, and ask how you can improve your own accessibility.
Reprimand them severely for going behind your back and making you look bad.
Ignore it so you don't seem insecure about your authority.
Ask your manager to direct the employee back to you next time this happens.

scenario: You inherit a team that was previously micromanaged and is now terrified of making mistakes. How do you foster a culture of innovation?

options.text: Explicitly state that small mistakes are learning opportunities, praise risk-taking publicly, and delegate authority gradually.
Tell them on day one that you are totally hands-off and they can do whatever they want.
Review their work just as closely as the last manager, but use a friendlier tone.
Host a workshop on innovation and creativity to inspire them.

scenario: Your team has to work over the weekend to hit a critical deadline. They are exhausted. How do you lead them through the crunch?

options.text: Work alongside them, ensure meals are provided, and clearly communicate the comp-time they will receive once the project is submitted.
Tell them to work the weekend while you monitor your email from home.
Remind them that this is what it takes to be successful in this industry.
Apologize repeatedly throughout the weekend for making them work.

scenario: An employee consistently produces great work but has a highly abrasive communication style that upsets colleagues. How do you address it?

options.text: Provide specific, recent examples of their abrasive tone in private, explain the impact on the team, and set clear expectations for behavioral change.
Overlook the behavior because they are a top performer and losing them would hurt metrics.
Hint at the issue by sending them articles on emotional intelligence.
Address the whole team about 'professional communication' without singling them out.

scenario: Your company launches a new strategic vision that your team doesn't believe in. As a leader, how do you align them?

options.text: Translate the high-level corporate vision into specific, meaningful impacts for your team's day-to-day work, helping them find personal relevance in the goal.
Agree with the team that the vision is silly, but insist they pretend to care to keep upper management happy.
Print out the vision statement and hang it in the office, hoping it sinks in over time.
Focus on the parts of the vision they like and ignore the controversial parts.

scenario: You are leading a cross-departmental task force. Members from other departments are not prioritizing your tasks. How do you exert influence without formal authority?

options.text: Meet with each member to understand their department's goals, and find ways to align the task force's objectives with their mutual success.
Complain to their respective managers that they are not doing their assigned work.
Do the work yourself to ensure the task force meets its deadline.
Host a kickoff meeting to remind everyone of the importance of the project and secure verbal commitments.

scenario: One of your employees is consistently 15 minutes late. It's not impacting their output, but other team members are complaining about favoritism. How do you handle it?

options.text: Discuss the tardiness with the employee, explaining how it impacts team perception, and either agree on a flex-schedule or enforce the standard start time.
Ignore the complaints, as output is the only thing that truly matters.
Send a team-wide email reminding everyone of the official start time.
Tell the complaining team members to mind their own business and focus on their own work.

scenario: A team member frequently takes credit for ideas generated by others during meetings. How do you intervene effectively?

options.text: In the moment, gently redirect credit ('Thanks for highlighting Sarah's point from earlier'). Afterwards, address the pattern privately with the employee.
Call them out sharply in front of everyone so they never do it again.
Say nothing in the meeting, but quietly reassure the true idea-generator later.
Privately ask the true idea-generators to speak up more aggressively next time.

scenario: You are managing an employee who is significantly older and more experienced than you. They often second-guess your decisions. How do you establish your leadership?

options.text: Acknowledge their deep expertise, seek their input on complex issues privately to build respect, but remain firm in your final decision-making authority.
Assert your dominance by overriding their suggestions publicly to prove you are the boss.
Defer to their judgment on almost everything to avoid conflict.
Have a frank conversation asking them to stop challenging you in front of the team.

scenario: You have an idea for a new workflow that will save time, but it requires upfront effort to build. How do you pitch it to your skeptical team?

options.text: Run a small-scale pilot with one willing team member to generate data and prove the concept before asking the whole team to adopt it.
Mandate the new workflow immediately; they will thank you once they see it works.
Present the idea and ask for a team vote. If they say no, drop it.
Host a presentation detailing all the theoretical benefits and ask for their trust.

scenario: A key vendor is consistently underperforming, causing your team to miss deadlines. You have no direct authority over the vendor. How do you influence them to improve?

options.text: Schedule a collaborative review meeting with the vendor to discuss the pain points, review SLA metrics, and jointly develop a recovery plan.
Threaten to terminate the contract immediately if they don't fix the issues by tomorrow.
Complain to your manager and ask them to handle the vendor negotiations.
Send an email outlining all their failures and ask for a written explanation.

scenario: You want to build a culture of accountability where team members own their mistakes without fear. How do you start?

options.text: Model the behavior by openly sharing a mistake you recently made, what you learned, and how you fixed it.
Implement a strict penalty system for recurring errors to force accountability.
Add 'Accountability' as an agenda item to every weekly meeting.
Praise team members publicly when they successfully complete their tasks on time.

scenario: A new hire is struggling to keep up with the workload but insists they are fine when you ask. How do you provide support without seeming overbearing?

options.text: Review their workload with them, point out specific areas where you see bottlenecks, and offer targeted coaching or adjustments.
Take them at their word; if they say they are fine, they need to figure it out.
Reassign some of their tasks to other team members without telling them.
Pair them with a senior mentor on the team to help them get up to speed informally.

scenario: Your team just achieved a major milestone, but they are immediately faced with another massive project. How do you handle the transition?

options.text: Pause to meaningfully celebrate the milestone, highlight specific individual contributions, and give the team a breather before kicking off the next project.
Briefly say 'good job' in an email and immediately send out the assignments for the new project.
Delay the start of the next project by a week without telling management, to give the team a break.
Host a quick celebratory lunch while simultaneously presenting the kickoff for the new project.

scenario: You notice your team is experiencing 'change fatigue' from constant organizational restructuring. How do you lead them through this?

options.text: Act as a filter, prioritizing which changes need immediate action, maintaining stable team routines where possible, and actively listening to their concerns.
Tell them to stop complaining because change is the only constant in business.
Ignore the corporate restructuring directives entirely until the team feels less stressed.
Hold a meeting to let everyone vent their frustrations, then ask them to try their best to keep up.

scenario: You have a brilliant but highly cynical employee who shoots down every new idea in brainstorms. How do you redirect this energy?

options.text: Assign them the role of 'Risk Analyst' in discussions, framing their cynicism as a strength to identify flaws, but requiring them to also propose solutions.
Stop inviting them to brainstorming sessions to protect the team's creative energy.
Argue back with them in front of the team to prove their negativity is unfounded.
Speak to them privately and ask them to limit their negative comments to one per meeting.

scenario: A rumor is circulating that layoffs are coming, causing severe anxiety on your team. You know the rumors are partially true but aren't authorized to share details yet. What do you do?

options.text: Acknowledge the rumors openly, clarify what you know and don't know (or can't share yet), and commit to sharing concrete information the moment you are able.
Deny the rumors completely to keep the team focused and calm.
Tell the team secretly what you know, asking them to promise not to tell anyone else.
Refuse to comment on rumors and abruptly change the subject back to work tasks.

scenario: As a newly promoted manager, you are overwhelmed with your new administrative duties but are reluctant to hand over your previous technical tasks because you can do them faster than anyone else. How do you proceed?

options.text: Identify the technical tasks that would be good development opportunities for your team, train them, and gradually hand them over so you can focus on managing.
Continue doing the technical tasks by working late, as it's unfair to burden your team with your old work.
Quickly assign all your old technical tasks to the most experienced team member without much training.
Keep the most critical technical tasks for yourself and delegate the easier, less important ones to your team.

scenario: You need to delegate a complex reporting task. The best person for the job is already working at full capacity, while a junior member has free time but lacks experience. What do you do?

options.text: Assign the task to the junior member, clearly explain the expectations, and set up frequent check-ins to provide guidance and support.
Give the task to the experienced person and tell them they need to figure out how to manage their time better.
Do the reporting task yourself so it gets done correctly without stressing anyone on the team.
Have the junior member do the initial data gathering, and ask the experienced member to finalize the complex parts.

scenario: A team member comes to you with a problem they are perfectly capable of solving themselves. They ask you what they should do. How do you respond to empower them?

options.text: Ask them, 'What do you think is the best approach?' and guide them to trust their own judgment.
Tell them exactly step-by-step what to do so they don't make a mistake.
Tell them you are busy and that they need to figure it out on their own.
Suggest two possible solutions and let them choose which one they want to execute.

scenario: You delegated a project to a capable employee, but you catch yourself constantly checking their progress and correcting minor stylistic choices. How should you adjust your approach?

options.text: Step back, focus only on the final outcomes and agreed-upon milestones, and allow them to complete the work their way.
Take the project back, as your anxiety over the details indicates it shouldn't have been delegated yet.
Apologize for micromanaging but ask them to copy you on all emails so you can passively monitor.
Schedule a brief daily 15-minute stand-up so you can stay informed without hovering over their desk.

scenario: Your team needs to present a quarterly update to senior leadership. Normally you do this, but you want to empower a high-performing team member. How do you handle this?

options.text: Delegate the presentation to them, help them prep, and publicly support them during the meeting while letting them own the spotlight.
Keep doing the presentation yourself to ensure it's flawless for senior leadership.
Let them build the slide deck, but you deliver the actual presentation so they learn by watching.
Split the presentation 50/50 so they get exposure but you still maintain a strong presence.

scenario: An employee makes a significant mistake on a task you delegated to them. They are very upset. What is the most empowering way to handle this?

options.text: Review the mistake with them, focusing on what happened and how to fix it, and ask them to propose a plan to prevent it next time.
Reprimand them for the error and reassign the task to someone more reliable.
Fix the mistake yourself quietly so they don't feel worse about it.
Reassure them that mistakes happen, fix the issue together, and supervise their next few attempts closely.

scenario: You have a batch of tedious, repetitive administrative tasks that need to be done every week. How do you delegate this fairly?

options.text: Create a rotating schedule where everyone on the team, including yourself, takes a turn completing the tasks.
Assign all the administrative work permanently to the newest or lowest-ranking team member.
Do it all yourself because it's not fair to waste your team's valuable time on grunt work.
Ask for volunteers each week and assign it to whoever raises their hand.

scenario: When delegating a new project, you want to ensure the employee fully understands the expectations without feeling talked down to. How do you ensure alignment?

options.text: Explain the goal and constraints, then ask the employee to summarize their understanding of the deliverables and the approach they plan to take.
Give them a 10-page highly detailed manual and tell them not to deviate from it.
Give them a brief overview and just tell them to ask questions if they get stuck.
Outline the project goals and schedule a follow-up meeting in two days to review their initial project plan.

scenario: An employee repeatedly brings a delegated task back to you, asking you to review it at every minor step, effectively practicing 'reverse delegation.' How do you respond?

options.text: Clarify that they have the authority to make these minor decisions and establish specific milestones for when you will review the work.
Just review it for them quickly every time, as it only takes a few minutes of your day.
Refuse to look at it at all until the final deadline to force them to be independent.
Tell them you trust their work, but briefly glance at it anyway to give them peace of mind.

scenario: You need to delegate a task that you have never actually done yourself, so you don't know the exact steps. How do you empower your team member to take it on?

options.text: Share the desired outcome, admit you haven't done it yourself, and empower them to research and determine the best process, offering support along the way.
Don't delegate it; spend the weekend learning how to do it yourself first so you don't look incompetent.
Delegate it but pretend you know how to do it, vaguely telling them to 'figure it out.'
Give it to them and suggest they find someone in another department who knows how to do it for guidance.

scenario: A highly capable employee finishes their work early and asks for more responsibility. What is the best way to empower them?

options.text: Discuss their career goals and delegate a stretch assignment that challenges them and aligns with their desired development path.
Tell them to just relax or browse the internet since they worked hard and earned the downtime.
Give them the routine busywork that the rest of the team hates doing.
Ask them to help their peers finish their standard daily tasks.

scenario: You delegated the organizing of a client event to an employee. They want to book a venue you personally dislike, though it meets all budget and logistical criteria. What do you do?

options.text: Approve the venue. It meets the criteria, and true delegation means accepting that they might make different choices than you would.
Veto the venue and pick the one you prefer to ensure the event meets your personal standards.
Hint strongly that it’s a bad idea until they change their mind and pick something else.
Ask them to find three more options just to make absolutely sure it’s the best choice, delaying the process.

scenario: Your team is transitioning to a hybrid work model. How do you adapt your delegation strategy to empower remote employees?

options.text: Focus heavily on clear, documented outcomes and deadlines, giving them the autonomy to manage their own schedules to achieve those results.
Require them to be on a continuous video call all day so you can ensure they are actually working on delegated tasks.
Only delegate important tasks to the employees who come into the office where you can see them.
Schedule multiple check-ins throughout the day via chat to ensure they aren't stuck on anything.

scenario: You need to delegate a high-stakes project. Two competitive team members both want it. How do you handle this to maintain team morale and empowerment?

options.text: Evaluate their current workloads and skills, assign the project to the best fit, and find a different meaningful development opportunity for the other.
Let them argue it out and give it to whoever fights hardest for it.
Do the project yourself so neither of them gets jealous.
Force them to co-lead the project, even if the project is too small for two leaders.

scenario: You are going on a two-week vacation and won't have email access. How do you empower your team to handle operations in your absence?

options.text: Designate a point person for emergencies, clearly define decision-making boundaries for the team, and notify stakeholders of who is in charge.
Tell the team to put all major decisions on hold until you return, to avoid any mistakes.
Just leave without assigning roles; they are adults and will figure it out organically.
Ask your own manager to step in and directly supervise your team while you are gone.

scenario: A delegated project is falling behind schedule. The employee hasn't asked for help. What is your most effective action?

options.text: Check in with them, note the timeline slip in a supportive tone, and ask if there are roadblocks you can help clear.
Publicly call them out in a team meeting for missing deadlines to ensure it doesn't happen again.
Silently extend the deadline without telling them, assuming they just need more time.
Step in and take over a portion of their work to ensure it gets done on time.

scenario: An employee feels they are being 'dumped on' with extra work rather than being 'empowered' through delegation. How do you address their perception?

options.text: Meet to review their workload, explain how these specific tasks align with their career goals, and re-balance tasks if they are genuinely over capacity.
Tell them that entry-level management means doing what you're told without complaining.
Immediately take back all the delegated tasks and apologize for burdening them.
Explain that everyone has to do more with less right now and promise it will get better soon.

scenario: Your team deals with customer complaints, and they constantly escalate minor issues to you for approval to offer a $20 refund. How do you empower them?

options.text: Establish a policy that gives team members the authority to issue refunds up to $50 without your approval, and train them on the criteria.
Tell them to stop bothering you and just reject all refund requests.
Continue approving them yourself to ensure the company doesn't lose too much money.
Tell them they can approve refunds, but they must message you immediately after each one so you can review their decision.

scenario: You delegated the drafting of a critical email to a stakeholder. The employee sends you a draft that is okay, but not in your 'voice.' What do you do?

options.text: Check if it clearly communicates the necessary points accurately and professionally; if yes, approve it. Allow them to have their own voice.
Rewrite the entire email so it sounds exactly like something you would have written.
Tell them it's terrible and make them rewrite it until it matches your personal style.
Make a few minor stylistic tweaks to make it slightly closer to your voice before sending.

scenario: A team member successfully completed a highly challenging delegated task, saving you hours of work. How do you recognize this?

options.text: Praise them specifically in front of the team, detail the impact of their work, and ensure your manager knows about their success.
Take the credit for the success since you were the manager who directed the project.
Just say 'thanks' in passing so they don't get an inflated ego.
Send them a private 'good job' email and assign them their next task.

scenario: You want to empower your team to run the weekly staff meeting, instead of you dictating the agenda every time. How do you implement this?

options.text: Create a rotating schedule where a different team member sets the agenda and chairs the meeting each week, offering guidance if they request it.
Stop showing up to the meetings entirely so they are forced to run them.
Tell them they can run it, but step in and take over the moment there is an awkward silence.
Ask them for agenda items beforehand, but continue to lead the meeting yourself.

scenario: You delegate a task to an older, veteran employee who used to do this job years ago. They are offended and feel you are treating them like a rookie. How do you handle this?

options.text: Apologize for the misunderstanding, frame the delegation as relying on their deep expertise, and ask them to own the outcome rather than telling them how to do it.
Remind them that you are the manager now and they need to do what is assigned.
Take the task back to avoid any further conflict with the veteran employee.
Tell them you are just following standard procedures for all employees, regardless of tenure.

scenario: Your team has identified a recurring bottleneck in their workflow. You want to empower them to fix it. What is your role?

options.text: Ask the team to collaboratively design a solution, provide them with any resources they need, and champion their proposed change to upper management.
Ignore them; workflow optimization is management's job, not the team's.
Design a new workflow yourself and mandate that they follow it starting tomorrow.
Let them implement whatever fix they want, but don't involve yourself in clearing the path for them.

scenario: You delegated a research task to a new hire. After a week, they have gone completely off track and are analyzing the wrong data. What do you do?

options.text: Meet with them to gently course-correct, clarify the initial objective, and adjust the check-in frequency to ensure they stay aligned going forward.
Fire them or put them on a PIP immediately for failing to follow basic instructions.
Take the task away from them and do it yourself since the deadline is approaching.
Point out the error and tell them to start over from scratch by tomorrow morning.

scenario: You need to delegate the onboarding of a new team member. Who should you empower to do this?

options.text: A reliable, mid-level employee who demonstrates strong cultural values and is looking for leadership experience.
The most cynical veteran employee, hoping the responsibility will improve their attitude.
Nobody; you must do 100% of the onboarding yourself to ensure it's done right.
The person who was most recently hired, since they just went through the process themselves.

scenario: A cross-functional project requires a representative from your team. You want to delegate this role, but it involves making commitments on your behalf. How do you empower your representative?

options.text: Clearly define the scope of what they can commit to without asking you, and assure them you will back up their decisions within those parameters.
Send them, but tell them to say 'no' to everything so your team doesn't get extra work.
Send them, but require them to text you for permission before agreeing to any point during the meetings.
Tell them to just gather information and that you will make all the actual commitments later via email.

scenario: You have noticed that when you are out of the office, productivity plummets because the team waits for your approval on minor steps. How do you fix this?

options.text: Identify the common bottlenecks, train the team to handle those specific approvals, and explicitly grant them the authority to proceed without you.
Never take time out of the office again so productivity remains high.
Scold the team for being lazy when you are not physically watching them.
Require them to call your personal cell phone for approvals even when you are on PTO.

scenario: You delegate the creation of a first draft of a report. The employee hands in a draft that requires significant editing. How do you respond to build their skills?

options.text: Highlight the strong points, provide specific feedback on areas needing improvement, and ask them to take a second pass at editing it.
Tell them they are a terrible writer and you will never ask them to draft anything again.
Heavily edit it yourself and submit it without showing them the changes.
Show them your edited version so they can see how it should be done next time.

scenario: An employee approaches you with a great idea for a new team initiative, but you don't have time to manage it. How do you empower them?

options.text: Tell them it's a great idea, ask them to draft a brief proposal and implementation plan, and offer to sponsor them to lead the initiative.
Tell them to forget about it because you don't have the bandwidth to oversee it.
Steal the idea and present it to your boss as your own when you have more time.
Say it sounds good and tell them to just start doing it in their free time without any formal structure.

scenario: You notice your team frequently defers to you during brainstorming sessions, waiting for you to provide the 'right' answer. How do you change this dynamic?

options.text: Start speaking last in meetings, actively ask open-ended questions, and intentionally champion team members' ideas over your own.
Continue giving the answers; it's why you are the manager.
Sit in silence until someone else speaks, creating an uncomfortable atmosphere to force participation.
Assign brainstorming topics as homework so they have to bring ideas to the meeting.

scenario: You delegated a technical troubleshooting task to an employee. They have been struggling with it for days but refuse to ask for help, wanting to prove themselves. How do you intervene?

options.text: Praise their persistence, but remind them that knowing when to consult the team is a key skill, and offer to brainstorm with them.
Let them keep struggling indefinitely; they have to learn the hard way.
Take the computer/task away from them and fix it yourself in front of them.
Assign a more senior employee to quietly shadow them and fix the issue without telling them.

scenario: You want to delegate the responsibility of training a new software tool to a team member who is an expert in it, but they hate public speaking. How do you empower them?

options.text: Discuss alternatives, such as creating a written guide, recording a video tutorial, or doing small 1-on-1 sessions instead of a large presentation.
Force them to do a live presentation in front of the whole department to help them get over their fear.
Don't train the team on the tool at all to avoid making the expert uncomfortable.
Have them write a script and you read it to the team.

scenario: A highly empowered team member makes a decision that aligns with the goals you set, but it causes a minor political issue with another department. How do you handle it?

options.text: Support your team member publicly and take accountability for the fallout, then privately discuss how to navigate inter-departmental politics better next time.
Throw the team member under the bus and tell the other department it wasn't your decision.
Revoke their decision-making authority completely.
Apologize to the other department and force your employee to go apologize to them as well.

scenario: You notice one of your team members quietly crying at their desk after a difficult phone call with a demanding client. How do you approach the situation?

options.text: Invite them to a private room, offer a tissue, validate that the client is difficult, and ask what support they need right now.
Pretend you didn't see anything to avoid embarrassing them, assuming they will handle it themselves.
Tell them that crying is unprofessional and they need to develop a thicker skin if they want to succeed in this role.
Send them a quick instant message asking if they are okay, but avoid talking to them face-to-face.

scenario: You are having an incredibly stressful day and a team member makes a minor, avoidable mistake. You feel a surge of anger. What is your immediate action?

options.text: Recognize your own emotional spike, take a short break to regulate your feelings, and address the mistake calmly later.
Snap at the employee immediately, as venting your frustration will show them the seriousness of the error.
Fix the mistake yourself quietly and hold a grudge against the employee for adding to your stress.
Tell the employee you are too stressed to deal with their mistakes right now and walk away.

scenario: A historically high-performing team member has seen a sudden, sharp drop in the quality of their work over the past three weeks. They seem distracted. How do you intervene?

options.text: Schedule a private 1-on-1, express concern for their well-being, mention you've noticed a shift, and ask if there is anything going on they need support with.
Immediately place them on a formal Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) because results are all that matter.
Ignore the drop in performance for a few more months, hoping whatever is bothering them passes naturally.
Remind them of their past high performance and tell them you expect them to get back to that level soon.

scenario: Two of your direct reports are having a loud, heated argument in the middle of the open office about a project deadline. How do you de-escalate?

options.text: Calmly interrupt, ask both of them to step into a conference room with you, and give each a chance to express their frustration safely.
Yell at them to be quiet or they will both be written up for unprofessional behavior.
Email them both from your desk telling them to stop arguing.
Walk over and tell them to drop the topic immediately and go back to their desks to cool off.

scenario: You have to give constructive feedback to an employee who is known to become highly defensive and take criticism personally. How do you prepare for the conversation?

options.text: Frame the feedback around specific behaviors rather than personality, acknowledge their hard work first, and use a calm, supportive tone.
Send the feedback in a harsh email so you don't have to deal with their emotional reaction in person.
Water down the feedback so much that they don't actually realize they need to improve.
Deliver the feedback clearly but quickly, and end the meeting before they have a chance to argue.

scenario: Your best employee suddenly hands in their two weeks' notice because they accepted a job at a competitor. You feel panicked and betrayed. How do you react in the moment?

options.text: Manage your initial shock, congratulate them on the new opportunity, and express appreciation for their contributions before discussing the transition.
Show your anger and tell them they are making a huge mistake leaving the team.
Act completely indifferent and immediately start talking about how to transfer their files.
Express a little disappointment but quickly shift to asking why they are leaving and if they can be convinced to stay.

scenario: After a grueling month of overtime to launch a product, the team is visibly exhausted. Management just assigned another urgent project. How do you communicate this?

options.text: Acknowledge their exhaustion and the unfairness of the timing, validate their feelings, and discuss collectively how to pace the new work to avoid burnout.
Tell them to stop complaining because having a job is a privilege and they need to push through.
Deliver the news apologetically, but don't offer any adjustments to the workload or schedule.
Try to hype them up with forced positivity, telling them how 'lucky' they are to get such important work.

scenario: An employee consistently complains about company policies, draining the morale of the rest of the team. How do you handle their negativity?

options.text: Meet with them privately to explore the root of their dissatisfaction, validate valid concerns, but firmly explain how their vocal negativity impacts the team.
Tell them if they hate the company so much, they should just quit.
Avoid them entirely and hope the rest of the team ignores their complaining.
Remind them of the positive aspects of the company during team meetings whenever they start complaining.

scenario: A normally quiet and polite employee unexpectedly snaps at you during a team meeting over a minor schedule change. How do you respond?

options.text: De-escalate the moment gracefully, then approach them privately later to check in, assuming their outburst is a symptom of hidden stress.
Snap back at them in front of the team to assert your authority.
Ignore the outburst entirely and act like nothing happened.
Calmly tell them in the meeting that their tone is inappropriate and move on with the agenda.

scenario: You made a significant error in a project timeline that caused your team to have to work the weekend. How do you address this with your team?

options.text: Take full accountability, sincerely apologize for the impact on their weekend, explain what you learned, and outline steps to prevent it again.
Blame the client for the timeline shift to save face with your team.
Apologize quickly in an email but avoid making eye contact or discussing it further.
Admit the mistake but remind them that everyone makes mistakes and they shouldn't dwell on it.

scenario: An employee confides in you that they have been diagnosed with a chronic illness that will require frequent medical appointments and causes fatigue. What is your response?

options.text: Express empathy and support, ask them what accommodations they might need, and assure them you will work together to balance their health and workload.
Tell them you are sorry, but remind them that their output still needs to remain at 100%.
Immediately report their medical condition to the entire team so everyone understands why they might be slow.
Offer support, but immediately ask HR to intervene because you don't want to deal with the medical logistics.

scenario: You notice that one of your team members is consistently left out of casual team lunches and inside jokes, and they look sad. How do you address this?

options.text: Check in with the isolated employee privately to see how they are feeling, and subtly initiate inclusive team-building activities that highlight their strengths.
Force the rest of the team to take the isolated employee to lunch immediately.
Assume it's just a personality clash and let the team socialize however they want.
Have a direct conversation with the popular team members, asking them to be nicer to their colleague.

scenario: During your busiest week of the year, an employee requests three days off because a close family member was in a serious accident. How do you respond?

options.text: Approve the time off immediately, express your deep sympathy, and assure them the team will cover their workload so they can focus on their family.
Deny the request because the business need is too high during this specific week.
Approve the request but make them feel guilty about leaving the team short-handed.
Approve the time off but ask them to check their email occasionally if possible.

scenario: Rumors of massive company layoffs are circulating. Your team is highly anxious and distracted, but you have no official information from upper management yet. What do you do?

options.text: Hold a team meeting to acknowledge the rumors, validate their anxiety, share that you don't have answers yet, but promise full transparency the moment you do.
Tell them they are being paranoid and to get back to work.
Avoid the team as much as possible so they don't ask you questions you can't answer.
Try to reassure them by promising that no one on your team will be fired, even though you don't know for sure.

scenario: A recent hire is clearly struggling with imposter syndrome. They are doing fine work but constantly apologize and doubt their abilities. How do you help them?

options.text: Regularly point out specific, concrete examples of the value they add, and explicitly discuss how normal it is to feel imposter syndrome in a new role.
Tell them their constant apologizing is annoying and makes them look weak.
Just say 'you're doing great' occasionally and hope they figure it out.
Assign them easier work so they stop feeling overwhelmed.

scenario: You receive 360-degree feedback stating that your team finds your communication style 'intimidating and cold.' How do you process this feedback?

options.text: Process your initial defensiveness privately, then hold a meeting to thank the team for their honesty and ask for specific examples of how you can improve your tone.
Demand to know who wrote the comments so you can 'clear the air' with them directly.
Ignore the feedback, assuming they are just overly sensitive.
Apologize via email and promise to be friendlier, but don't actively change your behavior.

scenario: An employee is visibly grieving after the sudden loss of a beloved pet. They are at their desk but clearly not getting much done. What do you do?

options.text: Express heartfelt condolences, validate that losing a pet is like losing a family member, and offer them the rest of the day off to grieve if they want it.
Tell them it's just an animal and they need to focus on their work.
Leave them alone entirely, assuming it's unprofessional to talk about pets at work.
Say you are sorry for their loss, but remind them of their deadlines for the day.

scenario: An employee is deeply upset because they were passed over for a promotion in favor of an external hire. How do you handle their disappointment?

options.text: Listen empathetically to their frustration without getting defensive, validate their feelings of disappointment, and later work on a clear development path for their future.
Tell them they didn't deserve it anyway and list all their flaws.
Blame upper management for the decision so the employee doesn't direct their anger at you.
Tell them not to worry because another opportunity will probably come up eventually.

scenario: You realize you hold a personal bias against one of your team members because their bubbly personality annoys you, though their work is excellent. How do you manage yourself?

options.text: Acknowledge the bias internally, actively self-regulate your annoyance, and ensure you treat them with the same respect and opportunities as the rest of the team.
Micromanage them to find flaws in their work so you have an excuse to fire them.
Distance yourself from them completely, communicating only via email.
Tell them privately that their personality is too intense and they need to tone it down.

scenario: A team member uses heavy sarcasm in meetings. They think it's funny, but you can tell it makes others feel belittled and embarrassed. How do you address this?

options.text: Speak to them privately, acknowledge their intent might just be humor, but explain the negative emotional impact their sarcasm is having on colleagues.
Use sarcasm right back at them to show them how bad it feels.
Ignore it since they are just joking and no one has formally complained.
Address the whole team about 'workplace humor' without singling the person out.

scenario: An employee is paralyzed by anxiety over making a mistake, constantly seeking reassurance from you before taking any minor action. How do you lead them?

options.text: Have an empathetic conversation about their fear of failure, normalize mistakes as learning tools, and slowly build their confidence through small, independent tasks.
Scold them for being needy and tell them to grow up.
Just keep giving them the reassurance they want so they stay quiet and keep working.
Refuse to answer their questions entirely to force them to act on their own.

scenario: A team member confidentially shares that they are struggling with severe depression and it is making it hard to concentrate. How do you support them as a manager?

options.text: Thank them for trusting you, express deep empathy, ask how you can accommodate their workflow, and remind them of the company's mental health resources/EAP.
Tell them depression is a personal issue that should be left at the door when they log in to work.
Try to act as their therapist, offering life advice and diagnosing their triggers.
Suggest they take an immediate unpaid leave of absence until they feel better.

scenario: You manage two employees who clash: one is relentlessly optimistic, the other is deeply pessimistic and analytical. They frustrate each other. How do you manage this dynamic?

options.text: Meet with them together to highlight how their different perspectives actually complement each other, framing the optimism for vision and the pessimism for risk management.
Tell the pessimistic employee to smile more and stop dragging the team down.
Separate them completely so they never have to work on the same projects.
Tell them both to compromise and meet in the middle to maintain harmony.

scenario: You are dealing with a major personal crisis at home and are feeling emotionally drained. You have to lead an important, high-energy project kickoff today. What is the best approach?

options.text: Briefly and professionally mention you are having an 'off day' to set expectations, but rely on your self-regulation to facilitate the meeting effectively without trauma-dumping.
Cancel the kickoff meeting at the last minute without explanation.
Spend the first 15 minutes of the meeting venting about your personal crisis to get sympathy.
Fake extreme enthusiasm, though it comes off as inauthentic and confusing to the team.

scenario: An employee from a culture with very direct communication styles comes across as rude to peers who are used to indirect communication. How do you bridge this gap?

options.text: Have a private, culturally sensitive conversation with the employee about perception vs. intent, and facilitate a team discussion on diverse communication styles.
Discipline the direct employee for being disrespectful to their coworkers.
Tell the sensitive coworkers they just need to stop being so easily offended.
Advise the direct employee to stop talking in meetings and just communicate via email.

scenario: You notice that whenever you give an employee feedback, they immediately deflect and blame others to protect their ego. How do you break this cycle empathetically?

options.text: Reassure them of their overall value to lower their defenses, then gently point out the pattern of deflection, emphasizing that feedback is for growth, not punishment.
Yell at them for refusing to take accountability for their actions.
Stop giving them feedback to avoid the exhausting arguments.
Interrupt them every time they blame someone else and forcefully correct them.

scenario: A team member is sighing heavily, rubbing their temples, and making typos, but when you ask if they are okay, they curtly reply, 'I'm fine.' How do you proceed?

options.text: Respect their boundary in the moment, but gently mention later that your door is always open if they are feeling overwhelmed by their workload.
Demand they tell you what is wrong because their sighing is distracting the office.
Assume they are fine since they said so, and ignore the physical signs of distress.
Keep asking them 'Are you sure?' repeatedly until they finally crack and talk.

scenario: Your own manager publicly criticizes you in front of your team for a mistake you didn't actually make. You feel humiliated and angry. How do you model EI in this moment?

options.text: Maintain your composure, calmly state you'll look into the issue and follow up offline, and later address the public nature of the critique privately with your manager.
Scream at your manager in front of your team to defend your honor.
Agree with the unfair criticism meekly and apologize to avoid conflict.
Leave the room immediately, slam the door, and refuse to speak for the rest of the day.

scenario: A team member confides that they are going through a messy divorce. It occasionally causes them to be late or distracted. How do you balance empathy with performance needs?

options.text: Express deep sympathy for their situation, offer temporary flexibility with their hours, but clearly establish what core outcomes must still be met.
Tell them to get their personal life together because it is ruining their career.
Let them completely stop doing their work without addressing it, out of pity.
Offer sympathy, but refuse any flexibility because rules are rules.

scenario: An employee is returning to work after a three-month medical leave. They are nervous about catching up. How do you manage their reintegration?

options.text: Welcome them warmly, schedule a slow ramp-up period, provide a prioritized summary of what they missed, and check in frequently on their energy levels.
Drop three months of missed emails on them on day one and demand they catch up by Friday.
Treat them delicately like glass and refuse to give them any real work for weeks.
Give them a normal workload immediately, assuming they wouldn't return if they weren't 100% ready.

scenario: A team member consistently overshares intimate, uncomfortable details about their personal life during team meetings. How do you handle this with empathy?

options.text: Speak to them privately, kindly explain that while you care about their well-being, the level of detail is crossing professional boundaries for the team setting.
Humiliate them in the meeting by telling them they are being inappropriate and weird.
Let them keep talking because you don't want to hurt their feelings.
Start sharing your own inappropriate stories so they don't feel like the only one.

scenario: Your team worked incredibly hard on a proposal, but the client ultimately rejected it. The team is demoralized. How do you lead them through the failure?

options.text: Validate their disappointment, explicitly praise the specific hard work they put in, and frame the failure as a team learning opportunity rather than a personal defeat.
Blame the team's incompetence for losing the client.
Tell them to ignore the failure and just focus on the next client.
Apologize profusely and take all the blame upon yourself, acting like a martyr.

scenario: A reliable, quiet employee tells you during a 1-on-1 that they feel 'invisible' and undervalued because the louder team members get all the praise. How do you respond?

options.text: Apologize for making them feel unseen, ask how they prefer to be recognized, and actively commit to highlighting their specific contributions going forward.
Tell them they need to be louder and more aggressive if they want recognition.
Deny their feelings by listing a time you thanked them six months ago.
Start praising them excessively and artificially for every tiny task they do, which feels patronizing.

scenario: Two of your team members are arguing over who is responsible for a missed deadline. Both are blaming each other, and the tension is affecting the rest of the team. How do you handle this?

options.text: Bring them both into a meeting to mediate. Focus the conversation on uncovering the process breakdown rather than assigning blame, and collaboratively develop a plan to prevent it next time.
Review their job descriptions and unilaterally decide who was officially at fault, then issue a formal warning to that person.
Tell them both to figure it out and stop acting like children, or they will both be penalized.
Meet with each of them separately to hear their side, then send an email outlining a new process they must follow going forward.

scenario: Your team relies on another department for monthly reports. The other department's manager has been consistently late delivering them, and your team is getting frustrated. How do you resolve this cross-functional conflict?

options.text: Schedule a collaborative meeting with the other manager to discuss the impact of the delays, understand their roadblocks, and agree on a mutually feasible timeline.
Send a strongly worded email copying their director, pointing out that their delays are severely impacting company goals.
Complain about the other department to your team, showing solidarity with their frustration.
Ask the other manager informally over coffee if there is any way they can speed up the process this month.

scenario: An experienced, highly tenured employee refuses to adopt a new software tool you just rolled out, causing friction with younger employees who have embraced it. How do you handle this?

options.text: Meet privately with the tenured employee to understand their specific reservations, offer customized training, and explain how the tool benefits the whole team's workflow.
Tell the employee that using the new tool is mandatory and their refusal will be reflected in their next performance review.
Let the tenured employee keep using the old system to avoid upsetting them, even if it causes minor delays.
Pair them with a younger employee to act as their 'tech tutor' so they can learn it peer-to-peer.

scenario: Two employees have drastically different communication styles. One is direct and blunt, while the other is sensitive and feels constantly attacked. This is causing a breakdown in their collaboration. What is your approach?

options.text: Facilitate a joint conversation focusing on communication preferences, helping them understand each other's intent versus impact, and set ground rules for future interactions.
Tell the direct employee to be nicer and tell the sensitive employee to develop a thicker skin.
Reassign their projects so they no longer have to work together.
Speak to them individually, coaching the direct employee on tact and the sensitive employee on assuming positive intent.

scenario: Three team members all requested the same highly sought-after holiday week off, but you can only approve one due to coverage requirements. They are currently arguing over who 'deserves' it most. How do you resolve this?

options.text: Hold a brief meeting to transparently explain the coverage constraint, review the documented PTO policy (e.g., seniority, first-come-first-serve), and apply the rule objectively.
Deny all three requests to ensure no one feels favorited, and require them all to work.
Give the time off to your top performer as a reward for their hard work.
Ask them to sit in a room together and figure out a compromise among themselves before you make a final decision.

scenario: A team member comes to you complaining that their project partner is not pulling their weight and they are doing all the work. How do you handle this complaint?

options.text: Ask the complaining employee if they have addressed this with their partner directly. If not, coach them on how to have that conversation, and offer to mediate if it fails.
Immediately pull the underperforming employee into your office and reprimand them for being lazy.
Tell the complaining employee that part of teamwork is sometimes carrying a heavier load.
Schedule a project check-in with both of them to review the division of labor and reassign tasks clearly.

scenario: You overhear two team members gossiping about a third team member's personal life in the breakroom, which has caused visible tension in the office. What do you do?

options.text: Address the two employees privately, stating clearly that gossip creates a toxic environment and violates team values, and instruct them to stop immediately.
Send out a generic team email reminding everyone of the company's professionalism policy.
Ignore it, as policing personal conversations in the breakroom is overstepping your boundaries as a manager.
Speak privately to the subject of the gossip, letting them know what is being said so they can defend themselves.

scenario: Your top-performing salesperson is incredibly abrasive and condescending to the administrative staff, leading to complaints. You rely heavily on this salesperson's revenue. How do you intervene?

options.text: Meet with the salesperson to firmly state that their behavior is unacceptable, regardless of their performance, and outline specific behavioral changes required immediately.
Gently ask the salesperson to be a bit more polite, wrapping it in praise for their excellent sales numbers.
Tell the administrative staff to ignore the tone because the salesperson brings in the revenue that pays everyone's salary.
Implement a new policy where the administrative staff communicates with this salesperson strictly via email to minimize friction.

scenario: During a team brainstorm, two employees get into a heated debate over the strategic direction of a minor project, derailing the meeting. How do you regain control?

options.text: Interrupt the debate calmly, acknowledge the validity of both perspectives, and table the discussion for a separate, focused meeting with just the two of them.
Make a snap decision right then and there on which strategy to use to end the argument.
Let them argue it out in front of the team until one of them backs down.
Ask the rest of the team to take a quick vote on which idea is better to democratically end the conflict.

scenario: An employee complains that their cubicle neighbor plays music too loudly and takes personal calls on speakerphone, making it impossible to focus. How do you handle it?

options.text: Speak privately to the disruptive employee, explaining the impact of their actions on others, and request they use headphones and take personal calls in the break area.
Move the complaining employee to a different desk on the other side of the office.
Tell the complaining employee to wear noise-canceling headphones and focus on their work.
Bring it up as a general 'office etiquette' topic at the next team meeting without naming names.

scenario: A conflict arises between a fully remote worker and an in-office worker. The in-office worker feels the remote worker is 'never available,' while the remote worker feels 'left out of the loop.' How do you bridge this gap?

options.text: Establish clear, team-wide communication protocols (e.g., core online hours, mandatory meeting summaries) and facilitate a conversation between the two to rebuild trust.
Tell the remote worker they need to respond to all messages within 5 minutes to prove they are working.
Revoke the remote worker's work-from-home privileges and force them back into the office.
Advise the in-office worker to just be more patient and understanding of the remote work dynamic.

scenario: You are CC'd on an email chain where one of your employees and a key external vendor are exchanging increasingly hostile and unprofessional remarks regarding a billing error. What is your next move?

options.text: Reply privately to your employee instructing them to pause communication, then call the vendor directly to de-escalate and resolve the billing issue professionally.
Reply-all to the email, scolding both of them for their unprofessionalism and demanding they act like adults.
Do nothing. It's important for your employee to learn how to fight their own battles with vendors.
Draft a professional response addressing the billing error, send it from your email, and BCC your employee to show them how it should be done.

scenario: Two junior employees are bickering because they both feel they are being assigned a disproportionate amount of 'grunt work' compared to the rest of the team. How do you resolve this?

options.text: Conduct an audit of the team's task distribution, sit down with both employees to review the data, and either validate and adjust the workload or clarify the reality of their roles.
Tell them that 'grunt work' is a rite of passage for junior employees and they need to pay their dues.
Reassign all the grunt work to a different, quieter employee to stop the bickering.
Create a rotating schedule where everyone on the entire team, including senior members, takes turns doing the grunt work.

scenario: Two ambitious team members co-authored a successful proposal, but now they are arguing over who gets to present it to the executive board. How do you mediate?

options.text: Meet with them together to emphasize the joint nature of the success, and suggest they co-present, dividing the presentation based on their specific areas of expertise.
Flip a coin or draw straws to decide who presents, ensuring it is completely fair and random.
Step in and present it yourself to the executive board to avoid any further conflict.
Give the opportunity to the employee who has had fewer chances to present in the past.

scenario: During a peer review session, Employee A gives constructive feedback to Employee B. Employee B takes it personally, gets highly defensive, and storms out of the room. What do you do?

options.text: Check in with Employee B privately to de-escalate their emotions, then coach them on receiving feedback objectively while also checking if Employee A's delivery was appropriate.
Immediately write up Employee B for unprofessional conduct and walking out of a meeting.
Cancel all future peer review sessions, as they clearly just cause drama.
Tell Employee A to apologize to Employee B to smooth things over quickly.

scenario: You learn that a rumor is circulating that you heavily favor one specific employee over the others, causing resentment and conflict within the team. How do you address this?

options.text: Self-reflect on your actions to see if the perception has merit, actively ensure equal distribution of opportunities going forward, and address the team to reaffirm your commitment to fairness.
Call a team meeting and angrily demand to know who started the rumor.
Start being overly harsh to the 'favorite' employee to prove to the team that you don't favor them.
Have a private 1-on-1 with a trusted team member to gauge how widespread the rumor is before deciding what to do.

scenario: Two employees get into a heated, emotionally charged argument about politics in the office breakroom. The argument is making others deeply uncomfortable. What is your response?

options.text: Interrupt immediately to stop the argument, remind them that the workplace must remain inclusive and professional, and ask them to return to their desks.
Let them finish the debate, but send a team email later saying political discussions are discouraged.
Join the argument to support the employee whose political views align with company values.
Pull them both into your office and issue formal warnings for creating a hostile work environment.

scenario: A project manager from another team constantly attends your team's meetings and aggressively hijacks the agenda to talk about their own priorities. Your team is annoyed. How do you handle this?

options.text: Speak to the project manager privately before the next meeting, clarify the purpose of your team's meeting, and agree on a specific, limited time slot for their updates.
Publicly cut them off during the next meeting and tell them to stick to the agenda.
Stop inviting the project manager to the meetings entirely without telling them why.
Create a strictly timed agenda and distribute it beforehand, firmly enforcing it for everyone during the meeting.

scenario: Two of your subject matter experts are at a complete standstill, arguing over the best technical approach to a problem. Both have valid points, but the delay is jeopardizing the timeline. What do you do?

options.text: Facilitate a white-boarding session where both map out the pros, cons, and risks of their approach, then guide them to a data-driven consensus or make the final executive decision yourself.
Tell them to figure it out by end of day or you will choose a third, completely different option.
Side with the employee who has more seniority to end the debate quickly.
Bring in a subject matter expert from another department to act as a tie-breaker.

scenario: An employee approaches you, frustrated that a peer (who has no managerial authority) is constantly micromanaging their work and giving unsolicited 'orders.' How do you address this overstepping?

options.text: Meet with the overstepping employee to clarify team roles and boundaries, explaining the difference between offering peer support and dictating tasks.
Tell the complaining employee to stand up for themselves and tell their peer to back off.
Promote the overstepping employee to team lead since they naturally want to manage people.
Bring them both together and clarify the organizational chart, ensuring both understand reporting lines.

scenario: Employee A is upset because Employee B presented a successful idea in a meeting without giving Employee A credit for helping brainstorm it. Employee A feels stolen from. How do you resolve this?

options.text: Validate Employee A's feelings privately, then speak to Employee B about the importance of shared credit and inclusive language in team success.
Send a follow-up email to the whole team clarifying that Employee A also worked on the idea, to set the record straight.
Tell Employee A that ideas are cheap and execution is what matters, so they shouldn't worry about it.
Encourage Employee A to speak up faster in the next meeting so they don't get overshadowed again.

scenario: An employee is angry about a new schedule change. Instead of talking to you, they bypass you completely and complain directly to your boss. Your boss asks you to handle it. What is your approach?

options.text: Meet with the employee calmly to address their schedule concerns first, then clearly explain the importance of following the chain of command for future issues.
Reprimand the employee solely for going over your head, refusing to discuss the schedule until they apologize.
Ignore the chain of command issue completely and just give them their old schedule back to keep them quiet.
Ask your boss to come into the meeting with the employee so you can present a united front.

scenario: You notice a pattern of passive-aggressive comments, sarcastic emojis, and deliberately slow response times between two team members in the team's Slack/Teams channel. How do you intervene?

options.text: Pull them both into a virtual or in-person meeting, present specific examples of the passive-aggressive behavior, and demand direct, professional communication going forward.
Delete their sarcastic comments from the channel as soon as they post them.
Post a message in the channel telling everyone to 'keep it positive today!'
Message them individually and ask them what is going on, trying to play therapist to uncover the root cause.

scenario: A major error occurred on a project because two employees both assumed the other was handling the final quality check. They are now fiercely arguing over whose job it actually was. How do you manage this?

options.text: Stop the argument, take ownership as the manager for the lack of role clarity, and immediately work with them to document a clear RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) chart.
Assign the blame to the employee with the higher salary, as they should have taken the initiative.
Tell them both they are at fault and dock their performance bonuses.
Mediate the argument until they both agree to share 50/50 responsibility for the error.

scenario: A conflict arises between a veteran employee who prefers doing things 'the old way' with paper files and a new hire who is digitizing everything without asking, causing confusion. How do you resolve this?

options.text: Establish a clear, unified team standard for file management, incorporating the efficiency of the digital system while ensuring the veteran employee receives support in the transition.
Tell the new hire to slow down and respect the veteran's process.
Let them each manage their own files however they want, even if it creates two separate systems.
Host a meeting where the new hire presents the benefits of digital filing to try and convince the veteran to change.

scenario: Two team members actively refuse to collaborate on a new, critical project because of a personal grudge stemming from a project that failed two years ago. How do you move forward?

options.text: Meet with both together, acknowledge the past history, but firmly state that their current refusal to collaborate is unacceptable and outline the professional expectations for this project.
Divide the project perfectly in half so they can complete it without ever having to speak to each other.
Fire the employee who is holding the deeper grudge.
Require them to go to a team-building lunch together to work out their personal issues.

scenario: A high-value client complains directly to you that your employee was rude and dismissive on a call. When you ask the employee, they vehemently deny it and claim the client was abusive. How do you investigate?

options.text: Listen to the employee's account fully without interrupting, gather any written correspondence or call recordings if available, and focus on establishing objective facts before making a judgment.
Immediately apologize to the client and assign a different employee to their account.
Tell the client that your employee is a good person and would never do that.
Ask the employee and the client to jump on a joint call with you to hash out the misunderstanding.

scenario: You discover that a highly competitive team member is intentionally withholding crucial information from a peer in order to look better in front of upper management. How do you handle this sabotage?

options.text: Confront the competitive employee with specific evidence of the withheld information, explain that teamwork is a core metric of their performance, and issue a formal warning.
Start sharing the information with the peer yourself so they don't fall behind.
Praise the competitive employee for their aggressive drive, as it yields good individual results.
Remind the whole team in a meeting that 'sharing is caring' and information must flow freely.

scenario: Under the stress of a massive deadline, an employee suddenly snaps and yells at a peer in the middle of the office floor. The room goes quiet. What is your immediate action?

options.text: Step in immediately, firmly instruct the yelling employee to take a walk to cool down, and check in with the peer who was yelled at. Address the behavior formally once everyone is calm.
Yell back at the employee to establish dominance and show the office that behavior isn't tolerated.
Pretend you didn't hear it and let the team sort out their own stress.
Immediately pull the yelling employee into a conference room and demand an apology.

scenario: A minor compliance error occurs. Employee A made the error, but Employee B was supposed to double-check it. They are in your office arguing over who should take the blame. How do you handle this?

options.text: Stop the argument, explain that as a team they share the failure, and pivot the conversation entirely to how they will jointly fix the error and update the checklist.
Determine exactly who made the bigger mistake by percentage and allocate the blame accordingly.
Tell them it doesn't matter and just ignore the compliance error since it was minor.
Report both of them to the compliance officer and let them sort it out.

scenario: An employee makes what they thought was a harmless, sarcastic joke about a colleague's work habits. The colleague is deeply offended and complains to you. How do you address the joker?

options.text: Speak to the joker privately, focusing on the impact of their words rather than their intent, and clearly explain why the joke crossed a professional boundary.
Tell the offended colleague that it was just a joke and they shouldn't be so sensitive.
Laugh it off and tell the joker they need to be more careful about who is listening.
Ask the joker to publicly apologize to the colleague in front of the whole team.

scenario: Your department is split into two sub-teams. Both teams need to use a specialized piece of equipment to hit their goals this week, but there is only one available. A heated turf war is brewing. How do you resolve it?

options.text: Bring the leads of both sub-teams together, review the urgent priorities of the department as a whole, and collaboratively build a shared, hour-by-hour schedule for the equipment.
Give the equipment to the team that asked for it first, telling the other team it's their own fault for being slow.
Tell them to figure it out themselves, and if they can't, nobody gets to use the equipment.
Divide the usage exactly 50/50, even if one team's project takes three times as long.

scenario: Two of your best employees are in a conflict over a shared workspace. Both have valid, diametrically opposed needs (one needs complete silence, the other needs to make frequent sales calls). How do you resolve this?
