Take an unscheduled two-day sick leave without delegating your urgent responsibilities to anyone.

scenario: An employee is visibly cracking under pressure, making repeated mistakes and bursting into tears at their desk due to personal and professional stress combined. How do you support them resiliently?

options.text: Take them to a private space, offer empathetic support, temporarily relieve them of their most acute stressors, and connect them with company mental health resources.
Tell them that if they cannot handle workplace pressure, they should consider finding a less demanding career.
Pretend you don't notice their distress so you don't make the situation more awkward.
Send them home for the day immediately without checking their workload or offering follow-up support.

scenario: Your department undergoes its second reorganization in six months. Team morale is hitting rock bottom, and employees are openly expressing hopelessness about the constant disruption. How do you respond?

options.text: Hold a transparent town hall to validate their exhaustion, focus entirely on what is within your team's direct control, and celebrate small daily wins to restore morale.
Tell them that complaining is useless and they just need to accept whatever upper management decides.
Join in on their complaints about upper management to prove that you are just as cynical as they are.
Try to fake extreme cheerfulness, telling them that reorganization is an exciting opportunity.

scenario: You receive critical feedback from your director during a performance review that catches you off guard and feels harsh. You feel an immediate wave of defensiveness and discouragement. What is your reaction?

options.text: Acknowledge the feedback professionally, take time to process your emotions offline, and schedule a follow-up to discuss an action plan for your development.
Argue with your director aggressively on the spot, defending every single action you took.
Accept the harsh feedback silently, lose all your confidence, and withdraw from future leadership opportunities.
Nod politely during the meeting, but ignore the feedback completely once you leave the room.

scenario: A major technical system failure halts all work for your team right before a critical audit deadline. The team is panicking and looking to you for direction under high stress. How do you lead them through this crisis?

options.text: Take a deep breath to project calm, coordinate directly with IT on the fix, and assign offline contingency tasks to the team to maintain productivity and reduce panic.
Panic visibly alongside the team, confirming that the audit failure will ruin the department's reputation.
Send everyone home for the day without authorization because the system crash makes work impossible.
Tell the team to keep trying to use the broken system continuously, ignoring the IT outage.

scenario: You experience a personal family emergency that drains your emotional energy, but you have an important team presentation to lead the next morning. How do you manage your resilience?

options.text: Prepare your slides thoroughly beforehand, set strict personal boundaries for the presentation, and lean on your core content expertise to carry you through professionally.
Cancel the presentation five minutes before it starts without notifying anyone or arranging a backup.
Spend the entire presentation talking about your personal family emergency instead of the business topic.
Delegate the presentation to a junior team member at the last second without giving them prep time.

scenario: An employee is chronically overwhelmed because they struggle to say 'no' to extra tasks from other departments, leading to constant stress and missed deadlines on your team. How do you coach them?

options.text: Coach them on boundary setting and prioritization, and establish a rule that all cross-functional requests must be routed through you to protect their bandwidth.
Scold them for being unable to handle their workload and tell them to figure out their own time management.
Ignore their stress as long as your own manager isn't complaining about the missed deadlines.
Silently take over their extra tasks yourself every time they agree to do too much work.

scenario: Your team just completed an exhausting, high-pressure product launch that succeeded. However, leadership immediately assigns an even larger, more complex project starting tomorrow without giving the team a breather. How do you protect team resilience?

options.text: Push back with leadership for a brief 2-day operational pause to decompress, or structure a slow, low-intensity onboarding ramp for the new project.
Immediately launch the new project at full speed, ignoring the team's total lack of recovery time.
Refuse to start the new project entirely without telling leadership your reasoning.
Throw a quick pizza party to celebrate the old project while simultaneously handing out assignments for the new one.

scenario: You make a significant oversight in a report that gets exposed during a meeting with senior executives, resulting in sharp criticism. You feel humiliated. How do you recover your composure?

options.text: Own the oversight calmly in the moment, commit to delivering corrected data by the end of the day, and process the emotional sting privately afterward.
Burst into tears in front of the executives out of sheer embarrassment.
Blame a junior team member on the spot for compiling the flawed data.
Defend the flawed report aggressively, arguing that the executives are misinterpreting the numbers.

scenario: You notice an atmosphere of cynicism and chronic complaining developing on your team due to ongoing operational hurdles. It is dragging down team energy. How do you intervene?

options.text: Address the negativity constructively in a 1-on-1 or team session, validate real roadblocks, and shift focus toward problem-solving controllable challenges.
Threaten to write up anyone caught complaining about the company's operational hurdles.
Avoid interacting with the team to protect your own mood from their cynicism.
Tell them to smile more and try to maintain a positive attitude no matter how bad things get.

scenario: An important project you sponsored fails completely after months of effort. You are facing post-mortem reviews with stakeholders. How do you demonstrate resilience?

options.text: Lead the post-mortem with total accountability, transparently analyze what went wrong without making excuses, and present concrete lessons learned for future initiatives.
Refuse to attend the post-mortem review out of fear of facing the stakeholders.
Blame external market conditions entirely for the failure so your personal reputation remains intact.
Focus the post-mortem exclusively on minor successes to distract stakeholders from the overall project failure.

scenario: A high-performing employee is showing classic signs of impending burnout—working weekends, irritability, and declining work quality—but insists they are 'fine' when asked. How do you handle this?

options.text: Gently share your specific objective observations about their changes in behavior, mandate a reduction in their workload, and insist they take upcoming PTO.
Take them at their word since they said they are fine, and let them continue working themselves into burnout.
Punish their declining work quality with a formal write-up without addressing the underlying burnout.
Casually tell them to get some rest eventually while continuing to pile on new tasks.

scenario: You are managing multiple competing priorities, and your stress levels are causing you to become disorganized and forgetful. How do you restore your personal operational resilience?

options.text: Pause, clear your schedule for an hour to brain-dump and prioritize tasks using a matrix, and communicate realistic timelines to your stakeholders.
Keep working frantically on whatever is in front of you, dropping tasks randomly as you get overwhelmed.
Shut down completely, close your laptop, and ignore all work emails for three days without notice.
Ask your manager to take over your entire job responsibilities until you feel less stressed.

scenario: Your team has experienced a string of small failures and rejections over the last month, leading to low confidence and risk aversion. People are afraid to try anything new. How do you rebuild their resilience?

options.text: Reframe past failures as essential learning data, reduce the scope of projects to secure quick wins, and publicly celebrate safe experimentation.
Scold the team for being overly sensitive and timid about taking risks.
Stop giving them any challenging work, keeping them only on repetitive tasks indefinitely.
Tell them that winning is all that matters and they need to try harder to succeed.

scenario: You are dealing with an aggressive, hostile stakeholder who routinely yells during update calls. This is taking a heavy emotional toll on you and your team. How do you manage this stressor?

options.text: Establish professional boundaries by stating you will pause the call until communication remains respectful, and escalate the behavioral issue to your director if it persists.
Endure the verbal abuse silently on every call to avoid rocking the boat or losing the client relationship.
Yell back at the stakeholder with equal hostility during the update call.
Avoid taking the stakeholder's calls entirely, letting their emails sit unanswered for weeks.

scenario: You are juggling high-visibility projects at work while dealing with heavy caregiving responsibilities at home. You feel on the verge of exhaustion. How do you practice self-care and resilience?

options.text: Proactively communicate your temporary capacity constraints to your manager, leverage flexible work arrangements, and lean on delegation within your team.
Hide your home life completely and try to maintain 100% perfection at work until you collapse.
Complain to your team about your home life during work meetings to gain sympathy.
Let your work performance slip drastically without telling anyone why it is happening.

scenario: A sudden budget reallocation results in the loss of a contractor your team heavily relied on, increasing everyone's workload. The team is ready to mutiny. How do you guide them through this shock?

options.text: Explain the financial reality transparently, work with the team to de-prioritize non-critical deliverables, and absorb some of the administrative load yourself.
Tell the team that budgeting is out of your hands and they just need to work harder to cover the gap.
Join the team in protesting upper management's budget decision.
Try to secretly reallocate funds from a different restricted project account to keep the contractor.

scenario: An employee reacts to constructive feedback by withdrawing completely, going silent in meetings, and performing at the bare minimum for days. How do you handle their lack of resilience?

options.text: Check in with them privately, reassure them of their value, and gently address how their withdrawal impacts team communication and their own growth.
Ignore their silent treatment and let them sulk until they decide to get over it on their own.
Punish their silence by giving them extra undesirable tasks.
Apologize for giving them feedback in the first place to make them feel comfortable again.

scenario: You have a major presentation to senior leadership in one hour, and your computer crashes, wiping out your visual aids. Panic sets in. How do you manage your stress and salvage the situation?

options.text: Take a breath to steady yourself, switch to a whiteboard or a verbal narrative outline, and focus on delivering your core message clearly without slides.
Cancel the presentation immediately because you cannot present without your slide deck.
Spend the entire hour frantically trying to recover the file while keeping senior executives waiting in silence.
Ask a junior team member to quickly rebuild the entire slide deck from scratch in 30 minutes.

scenario: Your team is under intense scrutiny after an operational failure. Every move you make is being heavily audited by upper management. The atmosphere is tense and fearful. How do you build resilience?

options.text: Shield the team from unnecessary external noise, treat audit reviews as objective learning opportunities, and maintain a supportive, non-punitive internal culture.
Micromanage every single action your team takes out of fear that another failure will happen.
Blame the auditing process for slowing down the team and creating unnecessary stress.
Tell the team to ignore the auditors entirely and carry on as if nothing happened.

scenario: You feel a deep sense of imposter syndrome and chronic stress, feeling like you are unqualified for your entry-level management role. This stress is affecting your decision-making. What should you do?

options.text: Acknowledge these normal transition feelings, seek out a mentor or peer manager for guidance, and focus on continuous skill development to build competence.
Hide your insecurities completely and fake your confidence aggressively, refusing to ask for help.
Step down from your management role immediately because you feel stressed.
Vent your insecurities to your direct reports, asking them to reassure you that you are a good manager.

scenario: A sudden organizational restructuring places your team under a new director who has a vastly different, more intense management style. Your team is stressed by the transition. How do you lead them?

options.text: Learn the new director's expectations quickly, translate them calmly for your team, and act as an emotional buffer while helping your team adapt.
Complain to your team about the new director's style, fueling their anxiety and resistance.
Ignore the new director's style preferences and continue operating exactly as you did before.
Tell your team to bypass the new director whenever possible to avoid stress.

scenario: An employee is overwhelmed by a complex new assignment and wants to give up, asking you to take it back. How do you build their resilience?

options.text: Break the complex assignment down into manageable micro-steps together, reassure them of their capability, and coach them through the initial hurdles.
Take the assignment away from them immediately, confirming their belief that they are incapable.
Tell them they have to finish it alone because you don't have time to hold their hand.
Do half of the assignment for them secretly so they can meet the deadline without struggling.

scenario: You have worked through a grueling 12-hour crunch day to hit a milestone, and your personal energy is completely depleted. However, an urgent email arrives late at night requiring your review. What do you do?

options.text: Assess whether the email truly requires midnight action or if it can wait until morning. Protect your rest so you can operate resiliently the next day.
Force yourself to review it immediately while exhausted, leading to critical oversight errors.
Delete the email and pretend you never saw it until someone brings it up next week.
Forward the email to an exhausted team member late at night, expecting them to handle it.

scenario: Your team misses a key quarterly metric, and leadership expresses disappointment. Some team members begin pointing fingers and blaming each other. How do you restore resilience and unity?

options.text: Halt the blame game immediately, remind the team that success and failure are shared, and redirect their energy toward a collaborative recovery plan.
Allow them to argue and blame each other so the true culprit faces accountability.
Take the blame entirely upon yourself like a martyr, letting the team off the hook completely.
Dismiss the missed metric as unimportant and tell everyone to forget about it.

scenario: You are facing a wave of negative customer feedback that is eroding your team's motivation. How do you process this feedback resiliently as a leader?

options.text: Filter out the emotional hostility, extract objective operational insights, and present a constructive action plan to your team to address valid customer pain points.
Shield the team from all customer feedback so they never have to face negative comments.
Forward every negative customer review directly to the team to make them feel the pressure.
Dismiss all customer feedback as invalid complaints from unreasonable people.

scenario: An employee breaks down under pressure and threatens to quit on the spot during a busy workday. How do you handle this high-stress moment?

options.text: Invite them to step away from the work area to breathe and calm down, listen to their immediate stressors with empathy, and address the resignation talk after they have stabilized.
Accept their resignation on the spot and tell them to pack their desk immediately.
Beg them hysterically not to leave, offering them anything they want to stay.
Tell them they are being dramatic and to get back to work until the shift is over.

scenario: You find yourself dwelling on a past managerial mistake late into the night, leading to insomnia and high anxiety about your performance. How do you build psychological resilience?

options.text: Practice self-compassion, reframe the mistake as a normal part of the management learning curve, and outline a concrete corrective action for the future.
obsess over the mistake continuously, convincing yourself that you are unfit to be a manager.
Try to completely suppress the memory and pretend the mistake never happened.
Complain to your friends outside of work about how stressful your job is every single night.

scenario: Your department is given an impossible deadline by senior leadership for a major deliverable. Pushing back was unsuccessful. How do you rally your team resiliently?

options.text: Transparently share the immovable constraint, work with the team to cut scope to a viable MVP, and secure compensatory time-off for after the crunch.
Tell the team that leadership expects the impossible and they will just have to sacrifice their personal lives to make it happen.
Promise the team that you will secretly ignore the deadline, setting them up for failure.
Accept the deadline without adjusting scope, assuming the team will naturally figure out a way to pull off a miracle.
